The Plastic Tide

Everywhere, and not yet understood

We measured the tide before we understood the water. What microplastics do to us is genuinely unknown — which is not the same as safe.

2 min read4 figures, each sourcedWhere it is contestedCorrected onceUpdated 19 September 2026

In 2004 a marine biologist in Plymouth asked where all the ocean's plastic had gone, and gave the answer the name that stuck: it hadn't gone anywhere. It had gotten smaller.

If you keep one line

'Unknown' is not 'safe' — and a scary number with no methods section is not knowledge either.

ShareEmailXLinkedIn

Richard Thompson's one-page Science paper, 'Lost at Sea: Where Is All the Plastic?', reported microscopic fragments and fibres throughout British waters and sediments — and in archived plankton samples reaching back to the 1960s. He needed a word for particles smaller than the eye tracks and settled on 'microplastics'. Twenty years later the word is in treaties, and the particles are in deep-sea trenches, Arctic ice, table salt, and (by recent detections) human blood and placentas.

The scale question has real numbers. Global production went from about two million tonnes in 1950 to more than four hundred million a year now; Jenna Jambeck's 2015 estimate put roughly eight million tonnes entering the ocean annually from coastal countries, with wide error bars that nobody disputes matter less than the order of magnitude. Fragmentation does the rest: sunlight and mechanics grind macro into micro into nano, so the count rises even where the mass doesn't.

The harm question is where honesty gets hard. Detection is not toxicity, and the most famous number in the field (that you eat a credit card's worth of plastic a week) came from a 2019 advocacy estimate that later peer-reviewed work found overstated by orders of magnitude. The WHO's 2019 review of drinking water found no evidence of risk at current levels, while grading the underlying data poor — a sentence both sides of the argument quote in halves.

Then 2024 delivered the first hard clinical signal: a New England Journal of Medicine study found polyethylene fragments in the carotid plaque of more than half of surgical patients examined, and those patients went on to heart attack, stroke or death at roughly four and a half times the rate of the rest over three years. Observational, confounded, immediately contested — and impossible to wave away. The field's real bottleneck is unglamorous: cheap, standardised measurement. You cannot regulate, price or fix what you cannot affordably count, which is why the interesting work in water right now looks less like activism and more like instrumentation.

01By the numbers

2004The paper that put 'microplastics' into circulation; the word appears in marine-pollution work from the 1990s: Thompson et al., 'Lost at Sea: Where Is All the Plastic?', Science 304(5672), 2004 (bibliographic record, Europe PMC); Wikipedia, 'Richard Thompson (marine biologist)'
~8 MtEstimated annual flow of plastic into the ocean (Jambeck 2015; range 4.8–12.7)
4.5×Hazard ratio for cardiovascular events with plaque microplastics (NEJM 2024, observational)
2 → 460 MtGlobal plastic production, 1950 and 2019: Geyer, Jambeck & Law, 'Production, use, and fate of all plastics ever made', Science Advances, 2017 (2 Mt in 1950); OECD, 'Global Plastics Outlook', 2022 (460 Mt in 2019)

02How it happened

  1. 1907Baekeland's Bakelite — the first fully synthetic plastic.
  2. 1972Carpenter and Smith report plastic particles in the Sargasso Sea.
  3. 2004Thompson's paper in Science puts 'microplastics' into circulation.
  4. 2015Jambeck estimates ~8 million tonnes of plastic entering the ocean per year.
  5. 2019WHO reviews microplastics in drinking water: no demonstrated risk, poor data.
  6. 2024NEJM: microplastics in carotid plaque associated with ~4.5× cardiovascular events.

03Who did the work

Richard ThompsonCoined the word, built the field, and has spent twenty years telling both sides to calm down and measure.
Jenna JambeckPut the ocean-input number on the map with transparent arithmetic and honest error bars.
Raffaele MarfellaLed the atheroma study that moved the harm question from plausible to urgent.

04Where it is contested

Nearly every number. Lab contamination plagues detection; methods (spectroscopy versus visual counting) disagree; the credit-card factoid is advocacy arithmetic that peer review dismantled; and the NEJM result, the field's strongest clinical finding, drew immediate methodological letters. The honest position is double: the exposure is universal and rising, and the dose–response curve is still a blank axis.

05Corrected

Corrections are appended, never patched. What was wrong, and what is true now:

№ 13 · Sept 2026 · Who coined microplastics.

The Plastic Tide said Richard Thompson coined the word 'microplastics' in 2004, in its opening line, its timeline and its figures. The term appears in marine-pollution work from the 1990s; Thompson's 2004 paper in Science is what put it into circulation. The entry now says that.

06What I changed my mind about

I used to reach for the scariest number in the room. Spending time around water testing broke the habit: now I read the methods section first, and I have learned that 'we don't know yet' — said plainly, with the measurement plan attached — is more alarming to a serious listener than any borrowed statistic.
